citation: Murphy, Stephen; Hill, Tim; McDonagh, Pierre; and Faherty, Amanda (2023). Mundane emotions: Losing yourself in boredom, time and technology. Marketing Theory 23(2): 275-293. DOI: 10.1177/14705931221138617. (Note: title page spells the fourth author 'Amanda Flaherty'; the author-bio note at the article's end spells 'Amanda Faherty' -- treated here as the same person; apparent typesetting inconsistency in the source, not independently resolved.)
discipline: marketing / consumer research (semi-structured interviews analyzed via Thompson et al.'s existential-phenomenological method) applied to first-person COVID-19 lockdown accounts, informed by Heidegger's Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics
thesis: Using Heidegger's (1995) FCM typology of superficial and profound boredom, the paper asks how different temporal dynamics structured consumers' experience of boredom during the COVID-19 pandemic. It argues superficial boredom (situational restlessness, desire for distraction) is produced by a dominant temporal regime of digital connectivity (fragmenting/de-sequencing time) and acceleration (compressing time), which together trap consumers in a recursive loop between boredom and digitally-mediated distraction; profound boredom (existential discomfort with one's sense of self) arises instead from an abundance of uninterrupted, solitary time -- exactly the condition pandemic lockdowns exceptionally produced -- and, following Heidegger, Benjamin and Gardiner, is read as having 'utopian,' self-transformative potential, catalyzing participants' discovery of new tribal passions. The paper concludes boredom is neither purely negative nor purely individual, closing with an account of what it means to be 'bored together.'

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Situates the paper within tribal-marketing research on shared, dramatic consumer emotion (Cova and Cova's consumer tribes); notes the pandemic's disruption of tribal gathering (festivals, sport, live music, in-person exercise); coins the term 'mundane emotions' to name affective textures flowing from everyday routine; states the research question -- how do different temporal dynamics structure consumers' experience of boredom?

sections.title: Boredom in consumer culture
sections.summary: Reviews marketing/consumer research's treatment of boredom as a 'modern' mental state tied to individualization, self-actualization demands, standardization/homogenization, and the digital age's passive relationship to culture. Notes that when boredom is directly studied, it is framed as a negative state opposite to 'flow' that retail servicescape design must mitigate. Pivots to philosophy via Gardiner's observation that boredom can harbor 'subversive insight and the seeds of transformative praxis.'

sections.title: Heidegger on boredom
sections.summary: Expounds Heidegger's (1995) FCM account: superficial boredom (train-station/airport-lounge example; being held in limbo, left empty) and profound boredom (deep indifference to self and world; 'this boredom wishes to tell us something'). Discusses boredom's relation to time, rejecting a naive time-slows-down reading; situates the study within consumer-research temporality literature via Torres's 'temporal regimes.' States the pandemic's dual temporal situation (furlough vs. enforced home-working) as the empirical opportunity.

sections.title: Methods
sections.summary: 15 participants (Republic of Ireland and England, ages 20-60, mixed household types), 20 semi-structured phenomenological interviews (5 follow-up) across 2020-2021, 40-100 minutes each, transcribed verbatim. Iterative first-order coding (35 codes: e.g. 'social media consumption', 'lack of fun', 'time', 'distraction', 'restlessness') then second-order abstraction against Heidegger's typology and temporal-regimes literature, yielding three temporal regimes.

sections.title: Findings -- Superficial boredom
sections.summary: 'Experiencing superficial boredom' (Jenny: lockdown monotony, loss of festivals/tribal connection, turn to social media); 'Mundane social media consumption' (Paul: doom-scrolling as time-wasted-but-time-passed; Laura: mindless scrolling and regret); 'Connectivity' (Charlotte: smartphone distraction de-absorbs a couple from watching a film together, spreading boredom within the dyad); 'Acceleration' (Jamie: accelerated repetitive admin work leaving him drained onto social media; Mark: work/childcare time-pressure, Netflix bingeing).

sections.title: Findings -- Profound boredom
sections.summary: 'Experience of profound boredom' (Catherine: lockdown as 'dull Groundhog Day,' losing herself, questioning her identity); 'Consuming solitude' (Richard: 'an undifferentiated no one,' emptiness prompting self-questioning); 'Abundance of time and the discovery of passions' (Charlie: discovering a cooking passion; Darren: quitting a call-centre job, rediscovering cycling, pursuing a new career in recreation/sports management; Stephanie: discovering baking, turned into a side business).

sections.title: Discussion
sections.summary: 'Beyond tribal emotions and towards investigations of mundane emotions' situates the 'mundane emotions' contribution against tribal-emotion research's bias toward the dramatic. 'Boredom in an age of distractions' argues boredom is not simply negative -- profound boredom is 'utopian' and self-transformative -- while superficial boredom is the modal contemporary experience given the dominant connectivity/acceleration temporal regime. 'Being bored together' argues boredom can spread within a shared activity and that shared rejection of boredom/monotony (e.g., UK punk culture) has historically been tribe-forming. Closes flagging class/material conditions as an unaddressed limitation.

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: central positive construct: existential discomfort with one's sense of self that, following Heidegger's 'undifferentiated no one' and 'authentic being-in-the-world'/'moment of vision,' catalyzes participants' discovery of new tribal passions

constructs.label: being-bored-by (1st form)
constructs.treatment: the only situative form cited by name/example; train-station/airport-lounge case (held in limbo, left empty); this limbo-emptiness structure is applied, unaltered, as the template for all superficial-boredom interview extracts

constructs.label: being-bored-with (2nd form)
constructs.treatment: NOT TREATED -- Murphy et al. state Heidegger describes only 'two kinds of boredom,' omitting the dinner-party example and the second form's distinctive diffuse/pervasive quality entirely, even though some data (Charlotte's shared-film account) arguably fits this form better than the first

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: not treated in the psychometric/individual-differences sense (no scale, no state-trait literature); the authors' own 'situational'/'superficial' label is phenomenological, not psychometric, and risks terminological conflation across the cluster

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: not treated; no psychometric instrument of any kind used in this qualitative interview study

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: thin; cited only via Heath and Nixon's (2021) 'daydreaming' work, both as a symptom in the negative-boredom literature and as a parallel 'mundane emotion' gestured toward for future research; not analyzed in the interview data itself

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: not treated; outside this paper's phenomenological register

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: not explicitly cited (Elpidorou's regulatory-theory literature absent from the reference list), but structurally paralleled: the 'utopian'/generative reading of profound boredom runs in the same direction as a functional/adaptive account, reached via Heidegger/Benjamin/Gardiner rather than cognitive-psychological regulatory theory (P/anticipatory-application observation)

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: treated and contested; identifies 'boredom is the opposite of a flow state' (Mathwick and Rigdon, 2004) as the dominant consumer-psychology assumption underwriting servicescape-design efforts to eliminate boredom, and positions the paper's generative reading of profound boredom as a corrective to this purely deficit-based framing

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: central, load-bearing construct: lockdown imposed a 'Groundhog Day'-like monotony in which life 'appeared on pause'; Catherine's account of lockdown 'at its worst' as a 'dull Groundhog Day' with 'nothing exciting going on, day after day' is the clearest first-person instance

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: reframed via the paper's own 'temporal regimes' apparatus rather than Heidegger's threefold escalation: superficial boredom explained by connectivity (fragmented/de-sequenced time) and acceleration (compressed time); profound boredom explained by an abundance of uninterrupted time; explicitly rejects a naive time-slows-down reading of Heidegger's 'feeling of time' claim (citing Anderson, 2004)

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.treatment: semi-structured, phenomenological interviews (Thompson et al., 1989 existential-phenomenological method); N=15 participants, 20 interviews total (5 follow-up), ages 20-60, Republic of Ireland and England, 40-100 minutes each, transcribed verbatim, iteratively coded (35 first-order codes -> second-order themes); NOT a validated psychometric instrument, NOT physiological/behavioral. All other MEASURE-axis items (EEG variants, pupillometry, gaze/fixation, blink, HR/HRV, behavioral RT, predictive-processing model, ML classification) are absent -- purely qualitative interview study.

readings.claim: Heidegger describes two kinds of boredom -- superficial (being bored by a situation, e.g. a train station or airport lounge, held in limbo and left empty) and profound (a deep indifference to self and world in which time appears absent).
'This boredom wishes to tell us something' (Heidegger 1995: 135) -- profound boredom, though a malaise, harbors existential possibility and, per Benjamin and Gardiner, 'utopian' generative qualities.

Boredom's relation to time is not that subjective time feels like it slows down; rather, profound boredom was historically an experience reserved for those with the privilege of free time, raising the question of whether profound boredom remains possible in an era of ubiquitous digital distraction.
readings.stance: qualifies-FCM, gestures toward fcm-07's epochal question

readings.claim: In profound boredom, the potential for 'authentic being-in-the-world' opens up as people face themselves in a 'moment of vision' (Heidegger 1995: 295).
readings.stance: restates-FCM, page-locus uncertain (see Reading of FCM section)

readings.claim: A dominant temporal regime combining digital connectivity (fragmentation/de-sequencing) and acceleration (compression/speed-up) produces superficial boredom as the modal contemporary experience, trapping consumers in a recursive loop between boredom and digitally-mediated distraction that never resolves the underlying state.

Profound boredom arises from an abundance of uninterrupted, solitary time -- the condition pandemic furlough/lockdown exceptionally produced -- and catalyzes the discovery of new tribal passions with self-transformative, 'fresh start' potential.

Boredom is not simply a negative, purely individually-experienced state, as the dominant marketing/consumer-research literature assumes; it can be generative (profound boredom) and shareable/collective ('being bored together').

Superficial boredom can spread within a shared activity -- e.g., one partner's phone-distraction de-absorbing both partners from jointly watching a film -- revealing that boredom, though usually theorized as strictly individual, can be transmitted within a dyad or group.

Discovered passions are socially valued partly for their entrepreneurial/economic productivity potential, reflecting a broader socio-economic 'subjectivation' of non-work time as an untapped productive opportunity.

concepts.term: acceleration (compression/speed-up of time, after Rosa, 2013; Husemann and Eckhardt, 2019)

tensions.note: Heidegger's own distinction, reduced by Murphy et al. to a twofold typology that omits the second (dinner-party) form entirely; organizes the entire Findings section.

The paper's central discussion-section contribution: contests the dominant marketing-literature assumption that boredom is purely negative and something to be escaped/designed-away, arguing (via Heidegger/Benjamin/Gardiner rather than Elpidorou's regulatory-theory literature) that profound boredom in particular is 'utopian' and self-transformative.

Superficial boredom is explained as environment/structure-caused (dominant temporal regime of connectivity+acceleration); profound boredom's trigger is likewise environmental (abundance of imposed solitary time), but its payoff -- which specific passion is discovered, and what it comes to mean -- is agent-relative and individualized (cooking, cycling, baking); a hybrid position on this axis, structurally similar to bor-sec-08's (Hughes) position on the same axis.

tensions.axis: boredom as individually-experienced vs. boredom as shareable/collective
tensions.note: Contests the assumption (shared by the dominant marketing literature and, per bor-sec-08's critique, by Heidegger's own individualist framework) that boredom afflicts individuals only; argues boredom can spread within a couple/group via a jointly but unevenly attended-to activity, and that shared rejection of boredom (e.g. punk culture) has historically been tribe-forming.
